chunks: "Slope compensation is a small artificial ramp that is added to the sensed inductor current, or equivalently subtracted from the current command, in a fixed-frequency peak current-mode converter.
The ramp starts at zero each clock edge and rises through the on-time.
It's needed because without it, the error in the inductor current is multiplied by D over one minus D each cycle, so above 50 percent duty cycle the error grows and you get subharmonic oscillation.
With a ramp of slope m a, the high-side turns off a bit earlier when the current error was positive, and the multiplier becomes minus m2 minus m a over m1 plus m a.
If m a is at least half the inductor's falling slope, V out over L, then the magnitude stays under one for any duty cycle.
If m a equals m2 the multiplier is zero, so a disturbance is gone in one cycle.
So it's needed whenever the converter can operate above 50 percent duty, which includes any buck whose input can drop below twice its output.
Practically I'd use about half to one times m2, and I'd also use it below 50 percent, since it damps the sampling double pole at half the switching frequency.

The trade-off is that too much ramp makes the inner current loop less dominant, so the converter behaves more like voltage mode, and the peak current limit gets lower at high duty cycle, since the ramp eats into the threshold.
Many ICs have the ramp built in, tied to a minimum inductor value, so I check the datasheet."
